problems.title: Find Two Numbers That Add to a Target
problems.statement: Given an integer array nums and an integer target, return the indices of two distinct elements whose sum equals target. Exactly one valid pair exists, and the same index cannot be used twice.
problems.approach: Hash map of previously seen numbers
steps: Create a HashMap from number to its index.
Scan the array from left to right. For each number x, compute complement = target - x.
If the complement is already in the map, return its stored index and the current index.
Otherwise record x and its index, then continue. Store only after checking to avoid using the current element twice.
problems.interviewTip: Explain why you check for the complement before inserting the current element. HashMap operations are O(1) on average.

problems.title: Check Whether Brackets Are Balanced
problems.statement: Given a string containing only parentheses (), square brackets [], and curly braces {}, determine whether every opening bracket is closed by the correct type in the correct order.

example.explanation: Every closing bracket matches the most recently opened unmatched bracket.

steps: Create an empty stack of characters.
For an opening bracket, push its matching closing bracket onto the stack.
For a closing bracket, the stack must be nonempty and its top must equal that character; otherwise return false.
After the entire string, return true only if the stack is empty.
problems.interviewTip: Mention why a counter cannot handle mixed bracket types or nesting order.

problems.title: Maximum Sum of a Contiguous Subarray
problems.statement: Given a nonempty array of integers, find the greatest possible sum among all contiguous, nonempty subarrays. Negative numbers are allowed.
steps: Initialize currentSum and bestSum to the first element, which handles all-negative arrays.
For each subsequent element x, decide whether to start a new subarray at x or extend the previous one: currentSum = max(x, currentSum + x).
Update bestSum = max(bestSum, currentSum).
Return bestSum after processing every element.
problems.interviewTip: Be ready to explain why initializing to zero would give the wrong answer for an all-negative input.

problems.title: Longest Substring Without Repeated Characters
problems.statement: Given a string s, return the length of the longest contiguous substring with no repeated character. Treat Java characters as UTF-16 code units for this problem.

example.explanation: The substring "abc" has three distinct characters; any longer window repeats a character.

constraints: s may contain letters, digits, symbols or spaces.
steps: Start a window at left = 0 and maintain a map from character to its latest index.
Move right across the string. If the current character was seen within the current window, move left just past its previous index.
Update the character's latest index to right.
Update best with the window length right - left + 1; return best after the scan.
problems.interviewTip: Why use max when moving left? A previously seen character may be outside the current window.

problems.title: Merge Two Sorted Arrays into One
problems.statement: Given two integer arrays sorted in nondecreasing order, return a new sorted array containing every element from both arrays, including duplicates.

example.explanation: Compare the front elements and append the smaller one. Both occurrences of 3 are retained.

constraints: Both input arrays are sorted in nondecreasing order.
problems.approach: Walk both sorted arrays with two indices
steps: Create a result array of length a.length + b.length, and start pointers i and j at zero.
While both pointers are in range, compare a[i] and b[j]. Copy the smaller value into the next result position and advance its pointer.
After one array is exhausted, copy all remaining values from the other array.
Return the result. Empty inputs and duplicates work without special handling.
problems.interviewTip: Explain the loop invariant: the result prefix is always sorted and contains the smallest elements processed so far.

problems.title: Find the First Position of a Target
problems.statement: Given a sorted integer array that may contain duplicates and a target integer, return the index of its first occurrence. Return -1 if it does not occur.

example.explanation: The target appears at indices 1, 2, and 3, so the first position is 1.

constraints: nums is sorted in nondecreasing order.
steps: Set left to 0 and right to nums.length, representing a half-open search interval.
While left is smaller than right, compute mid without adding left and right directly.
If nums[mid] is smaller than target, discard the left half including mid; otherwise keep mid and the left half.
When the interval closes, left is the first index whose value is at least target. Return it only if it is in range and equals target; otherwise return -1.
problems.interviewTip: Ordinary binary search finds any match; the lower-bound variation deliberately continues searching left for duplicates.

problems.title: List Binary Tree Values Level by Level
problems.statement: Given the root of a binary tree, return a list of levels from top to bottom. Within each level, values must appear from left to right. Return an empty list for an empty tree.

example.explanation: Visit the root first, then its two children, then the next level's children in left-to-right order.

steps: Return an empty result if root is null; otherwise put root into a queue.
At the start of each level, save the queue size. Exactly that many nodes belong to the current level.
Remove each of those nodes, append its value to the current level, and enqueue its non-null left and right children in that order.
Append the completed level to the result, then repeat until the queue is empty.
problems.spaceComplexity: O(n) including the output and BFS queue
problems.interviewTip: The saved queue size separates levels. Without it, newly enqueued children would be mixed into their parent's level.

problems.title: Minimum Coins Needed for an Amount
problems.statement: Given distinct positive coin denominations and a nonnegative amount, find the minimum number of coins needed to make exactly that amount. Each denomination can be used any number of times. Return -1 if no combination exists.

example.explanation: Two coins of value 3 make 6. Taking 4 then two 1s would require three coins.

steps: Let dp[x] mean the minimum number of coins needed for amount x. Set dp[0] to zero and every other entry to an unreachable sentinel amount + 1.
For each amount x from 1 to the target, try every coin whose value is at most x.
If dp[x - coin] is reachable, consider dp[x - coin] + 1 and keep the smallest candidate for dp[x].
Return dp[amount] if it is reachable, otherwise -1. The zero-amount case correctly returns zero.
problems.interviewTip: Explain why choosing the largest available coin greedily can fail: for [1, 3, 4] and amount 6, greedy uses 4+1+1, while optimal uses 3+3.
